prize_parts.citation: for the development of general palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling is a complete chemical story: a specific, well-defined reaction class, made general through mechanism-driven ligand design (Buchwald's biaryl phosphines, Hartwig's hindered alkyl phosphines and carbene ligands, with the oxidative addition/amine binding/reductive elimination cycle worked out in detail), and now used daily in discovery and process chemistry to make aryl amines, one of the most common motifs in pharmaceuticals and materials. It meets the classic Nobel test of a method that changed what chemists can make, and it has had more than two decades of unambiguous independent confirmation. Attribution is unusually clean for a methodology prize: two independent groups, each with sustained ligand and mechanistic programmes, and a clear precursor (Kosugi/Migita tin-amide chemistry) that was neither general nor catalytic in the modern sense. The 2010 cross-coupling prize covered C-C bond formation and does not preclude this chapter, just as it did not preclude later recognition of metathesis or organocatalysis. In my view the discovery is overdue rather than early.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is an extension of a field already honored in 2010, so a committee wanting a fresh conceptual idea may see it as incremental, and Kosugi's 1983 precursor and Migita-type tin chemistry leave a precedence question that a two-name citation sidesteps rather than answers. There is also a real argument that the field has moved on and that the committee's attention is better spent on newer modalities with clear human-health impact, such as targeted protein degradation, where timing could be perfectly good in the next few years. Finally, a purely synthetic-methodology prize risks being seen as narrow beside the biomolecular and materials candidates that several colleagues rank first.

responses.point: Aili ranks targeted protein degradation first as a conceptually clean idea, hijacking the ubiquitin-proteasome system with a designed small molecule, that has opened undruggable targets, and proposes Crews, Deshaies and Handa to cover the PROTAC concept and the cereblon glue mechanism.
responses.response: I agree the idea is original and I ranked it in my own list, but I put it lower because the clinical and chemical picture is not yet settled: no PROTAC is approved, the credit is split between two mechanistically separate strands (heterobifunctional degraders versus monovalent glues, where the cereblon mechanism came out of thalidomide biology rather than rational design), and a three-name cut leaves out Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and Ito. A prize that has to pick between those strands now risks a citation that is either too broad or contested. I would not oppose it in a later year, but I do not think maturity and attribution are at the level of C-N coupling today.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks B023 first for its rich mechanistic chemistry (ternary-complex cooperativity, linker design) and, as a close second, B002, noting that C-N coupling is ubiquitous and mature but sits in the shadow of the 2010 prize.
responses.response: I share Aqvist's reading of B002 as fully mature, and I would like to press on the point about 2010. Heck, Negishi and Suzuki were honored for C-C coupling; the C-N reaction needed different ligand design and a different mechanistic solution at the amine-binding and reductive elimination steps, so it is a separate achievement and not a repeat. Where I disagree is on ranking B023 above it: Aqvist himself calls the three-person limit forcing an unresolved choice between Ciulli and Handa/Ito, and I would rather give the prize where attribution is already resolved. If the committee does go to B023, I think his structural argument favours Ciulli's inclusion.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks proton-coupled electron transfer first as a unifying physical-chemical concept spanning bioenergetic enzymes and electrocatalysis, with Mayer, Hammes-Schiffer and Nocera covering experiment, theory and application, and places C-N coupling lower at sixth.
responses.response: PCET is conceptually attractive and I take seriously that it is textbook material, but as a synthetic chemist I find the credited three less clearly delimited than he does: Meyer is a recognised originator, Nocera's contribution is largely catalyst design, and theory and experiment have developed in parallel instead of resting on one decisive discovery, so any three-person set is hard to defend as the achievement. C-N coupling, by contrast, has a single reaction, two independent groups and a direct line from the discovery to its use in medicines. I would be curious whether he sees a citation for PCET that does not read as a field and does not dilute the contribution of Meyer.

responses.point: Zou also ranks B002 first, as a general, ligand-controlled method with exceptional breadth of impact fitting the tradition of enabling synthetic tools, and regards a two-person prize as the cleanest configuration, with Kosugi's precursor the main allocation issue.
responses.response: I agree with the two-person configuration and the reading of Kosugi as a precursor. I would add that the citation should be worded around general catalytic C-N coupling, not around palladium cross-coupling broadly, so it plainly differs from 2010 and does not imply a priority ruling on the tin-based work. Where I would qualify Zou is on the next ranked choice: perovskite solar cells are still being resolved on stability and on credit among six strong contributors, which I think weakens them as a pairing for this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat C-N coupling as sufficiently distinct from the 2010 C-C cross-coupling prize, and whether a citation should acknowledge Kosugi and Migita.

Whether the support for targeted protein degradation (five top-three placements) reflects a better judgement of timing than mine, particularly if a way is found to split PROTACs and molecular glues across a two-part prize with at most three people.
Whether any second part could be added to a Buchwald-Hartwig prize without exceeding three laureates, since adding a second achievement would reduce the number of names available for it to one.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I am a synthetic organic chemist at Lund, and colleagues Heiner Linke and Emma Sparr are also at Lund, but none of the shortlisted candidates are connected to Lund, KTH, Chalmers, Tartu or my mentor Masamune from the profile.
